Bounded Ratio Reinforcement Learning

Yunke Ao ††thanks: Correspondence to: yunke.ao@ai.ethz.ch Affiliation: ETH Zurich    Le Chen ††thanks: Equal second author contribution Affiliation: MPI for Intelligent Systems    Bruce D. Lee 22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: ETH Zurich    Assefa S. Wahd ††thanks: Equal third author contribution Affiliation: University of Alberta    Aline Czarnobai 33footnotemark: 3 Affiliation: Dartmouth College    Philipp Fürnstahl Affiliation: Balgrist University Hospital    Bernhard Schölkopf Affiliation: MPI for Intelligent Systems    Andreas Krause Affiliation: ETH Zurich
Abstract

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has become the predominant algorithm for on-policy reinforcement learning due to its scalability and empirical robustness across domains. However, there is a significant disconnect between the underlying foundations of trust region methods and the heuristic clipped objective used in PPO. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing the Bounded Ratio Reinforcement Learning (BRRL) framework. We formulate a novel regularized and constrained policy optimization problem and derive its analytical optimal solution. We prove that this solution ensures monotonic performance improvement. To handle parameterized policy classes, we develop a policy optimization algorithm called Bounded Policy Optimization (BPO) that minimizes an advantage-weighted divergence between the policy and the analytic optimal solution from BRRL. We further establish a lower bound on the expected performance of the resulting policy in terms of the BPO loss function. Notably, our framework also provides a new theoretical lens to interpret the success of the PPO loss, and connects trust region policy optimization and the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM). We additionally extend BPO to Group-relative BPO (GBPO) for LLM fine-tuning. Empirical evaluations of BPO across MuJoCo, Atari, and complex IsaacLab environments (e.g., Humanoid locomotion), and of GBPO for LLM fine-tuning tasks, demonstrate that BPO and GBPO generally match or outperform PPO and GRPO in stability and final performance.

1 Introduction

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved breakthroughs across diverse domains  [27, 11, 17, 19]. Among DRL methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [23] remains one of the most widely adopted algorithms. The core design of PPO is motivated by Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO, [21]), which constrains policy updates within a “trust region” to ensure stable iterations. By utilizing a first-order approximation of the TRPO objective, PPO achieves the scalability necessary for training modern large-scale models. As a result, PPO and its variant GRPO are now widely applied to tasks ranging from robotics to large language model (LLM) fine-tuning [13, 2, 26].

Despite its empirical success, PPO remains largely heuristic: its clipped objective is not directly derived from the trust-region formulation it was intended to approximate. Instead, the design of the PPO objective was primarily driven by experimentation [23, 5]. Furthermore, most existing theoretical analyses of PPO’s performance improvement rely on the original TRPO or policy gradient formulation [21, 12, 4], none of which fully capture the nuances of the first-order loss used in practice.

Numerous variants have been recently proposed to improve PPO. Some works focus primarily on algorithm design and report empirical performance gains without formal theoretical contributions [3, 34, 28, 6, 8]. Other works extend PPO to specific domains (e.g., safe RL, non-stationary RL) without modifying the core PPO loss function [1, 14]. There are also PPO variants aiming at improving the PPO loss from a theoretical lens [33, 30, 31, 18]. However, similar to PPO, they also utilize TRPO theory without introducing novel theoretical frameworks or establishing superior performance guarantees. Consequently, there remains a substantial gap between the theoretical foundations and the practical policy optimization algorithms.

To address this gap, we introduce the bounded ratio reinforcement learning (BRRL) framework. Instead of constraining policy updates through KL divergence [9] bounds as in TRPO, BRRL imposes bounded ratio constraints on the policy likelihood ratios. This formulation admits an analytic optimal policy, which reveals a simple structure for policy updates. We establish the following contributions using the BRRL framework:

  • •

    We derive the optimal solution of BRRL and prove its monotonic performance improvement guarantees. We also demonstrate that optimizing the PPO loss approximately pushes the policy towards this analytic optimal solution.

  • •

    We establish a connection between BRRL and the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM).

  • •

    We propose Bounded Policy Optimization (BPO), which optimizes an advantage-weighted divergence from the BRRL solution. We also extend BPO to Group-Relative BPO (GBPO), mirroring the extension from PPO to GRPO.

  • •

    We provide a performance improvement guarantee for the policy attained by BPO in terms of the loss that BPO optimizes.

  • •

    We demonstrate strong empirical performance of BPO on MuJoCo, Atari, IsaacLab locomotion tasks, and of GBPO for LLM fine-tuning.

Overall, BRRL provides a principled perspective on PPO-style algorithms, suggesting that their empirical success arises from approximating an analytically optimal bounded-ratio update. By more directly approximating this analytically optimal bounded-ratio update, BPO achieves improved empirical performance (Figure 1).

2 Notation

Markov Decision Process (MDP): We consider an infinite-horizon MDP defined by the tuple (𝒮,𝒜,𝒫,r,d,γ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r,d,\gamma), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, 𝒫:𝒮×𝒜×𝒮→ℝ\mathcal{P}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the transition model, r:𝒮×𝒜×𝒮→ℝr:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the reward function, d0:𝒮→ℝd_{0}:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the initial state distribution, and γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) is the discount factor. Let π:𝒮×𝒜→ℝ\pi:\mathcal{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} denote the stochastic policy. We denote rt:=r⁡(st,at,st+1)r_{t}:=r(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1}). The goal of the MDP is to solve the optimization problem

maxπ∈Πη(π):=𝔼s0:∞,a0:∞[∑t=0∞γtrt],s0∼d0,at∼π(at|st),st+1∼p(st+1|st,at),\begin{split}\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\eta(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{s_{0:\infty},a_{0:\infty}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}\right],\,\,s_{0}\sim d_{0},\,a_{t}\sim\pi(a_{t}|s_{t}),s_{t+1}\sim p(s_{t+1}|s_{t},a_{t}),\end{split} (1)

which maximizes the expected discounted return under policy π\pi within the policy class Π\Pi. Let us denote dπ​(s):=∑t=0∞γt​P​(st=s)d_{\pi}(s):=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}P(s_{t}=s) as an unnormalized state visitation distribution [21]. Then the objective in (1) can be rewritten as η(π)=𝔼s∼dπ,a∼π(⋅|s)[rt]\eta(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi},a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}[r_{t}].

Value function and advantage: We define the value function of a state ss given policy π\pi as Vπ​(s):=𝔼s0,a0,…|s0=s​[∑t=0∞γt​rt]V_{\pi}(s):=\mathbb{E}_{s_{0},a_{0},...|s_{0}=s}[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}], and the Q-function Qπ​(s,a):=𝔼s0,a0,…|s0=s,a0=a​[∑t=0∞γt​rt]Q_{\pi}(s,a):=\mathbb{E}_{s_{0},a_{0},...|s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a}[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}], where the actions (excluding the conditioned a0a_{0} in the Q-function) are sampled from the policy π\pi. The advantage function is defined as the difference between them Aπ​(s,a):=Qπ​(s,a)−Vπ​(s)A_{\pi}(s,a):=Q_{\pi}(s,a)-V_{\pi}(s). As shown in [21], the expected return of the new policy π\pi in (1) with regard to an old policy π0\pi_{0} can be derived as

η(π)=η(π0)+𝔼s∼dπ,a∼π(⋅|s)[Aπ0(s,a)].\eta(\pi)=\eta(\pi_{0})+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi},a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}[A_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)]. (2)

where the advantage is evaluated under π0\pi_{0}, and the expectation is taken over dπd_{\pi} and π\pi.

Surrogate objectives: We denote the surrogate objective optimized by TRPO [21] as

Lπ0(π):=η(π0)+𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π(⋅|s)[Aπ0(s,a)]=η(π0)+𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρAπ0(s,a)],L_{\pi_{0}}(\pi):=\eta(\pi_{0})+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}[A_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)]=\eta(\pi_{0})+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho A_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)], (3)

where ρ=ρ⁡(a|s):=π⁡(a|s)/π0​(a|s)\rho=\rho(a|s):=\pi(a|s)/\pi_{0}(a|s) are the importance weights. In contrast to (2), Lπ0​(π)L_{\pi_{0}}(\pi) takes the expectation over dπ0d_{\pi_{0}} instead of dπd_{\pi}. In TRPO, π\pi is updated to optimize Lπ0​(π)L_{\pi_{0}}(\pi) with constrained KL-divergence from π0\pi_{0}.

3 Overview of Contributions

In this section, we present an overview of the contributions within this work, as shown in Figure 2.

Bounded ratio RL framework: We consider a policy optimization problem with bounded ratio trust region constraints from an old policy π0\pi_{0}, instead of the KL-divergence constraint of TRPO, as shown in Figure 2 (Middle Left). Specifically, with Lπ0​(π)L_{\pi_{0}}(\pi) defined in (3), the problem is expressed as

maxπ⁡Lπ0​(π),s.t.​  1−ϵ≤π⁡(a|s)π0​(a|s)≤1+ϵ,∀s,a.\max_{\pi}L_{\pi_{0}}(\pi),\quad\text{s.t.}\,\,1-\epsilon\leq\frac{\pi(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\leq 1+\epsilon,\,\,\forall\,s,a.~ (4)

Notably, this problem has an analytical optimal solution π∗\pi^{*}, which in many cases (as detailed in Remark 4.3) can be derived as

π∗​(a|s)=[1+ϵ⋅sign​(A~π0)]⋅π0​(a|s),\pi^{*}(a|s)=[1+\epsilon\cdot\text{sign}(\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}})]\cdot\pi_{0}(a|s), (5)

where A~π0:=Qπ0​(s,a)−μπ0​(s)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}:=Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu_{\pi_{0}}(s) is the median advantage. In particular, μπ0​(s)\mu_{\pi_{0}}(s) denotes the median of Qπ0​(s,a)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a) over π0\pi_{0}, such that for any s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, A~π0\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}} satisfies 𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[sign(A~π0)]=0\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\text{sign}(\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}})]=0. As shown in Figure 2 (Middle Right) and Figure 3 (c), this optimal solution can be explained as: if Qπ0​(s,a)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a) is higher than the threshold μπ0​(s)\mu_{\pi_{0}}(s), then take the highest probability within the constraint π∗​(a|s)=(1+ϵ)​π0​(a|s)\pi^{*}(a|s)=(1+\epsilon)\pi_{0}(a|s); otherwise, let π∗​(a|s)=(1−ϵ)​π0​(a|s)\pi^{*}(a|s)=(1-\epsilon)\pi_{0}(a|s). Threshold μπ0​(s)\mu_{\pi_{0}}(s) is selected as the median, s.t. π∗\pi^{*} is a normalized probability distribution (∑aπ∗​(a|s)=1\sum_{a}\pi^{*}(a|s)=1). A formal theorem on the optimal solution for general cases is provided in Theorem 4.1. Note that Theorem 4.1 can also be extended to problems with asymmetric bounded ratio constraints (cl≤π⁡(a|s)/π0​(a|s)≤chc_{l}\leq\pi(a|s)/\pi_{0}(a|s)\leq c_{h}). This asymmetric solution is used to draw a connection to the cross-entropy method (CEM) in Section 4.6.

Monotonic performance guarantee: For the cases where optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} from (5) is optimal, it can be shown to have improved performance over π0\pi_{0}

η⁡(π∗)=η⁡(π0)+ϵ​𝔼s∼dπ∗,a∼π0​[sign​(A~π0)​A~π0]:=η⁡(π0)+ϵ​B,\eta(\pi^{*})=\eta(\pi_{0})+\epsilon\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi^{*}},a\sim\pi_{0}}[\text{sign}(\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}})\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}]:=\eta(\pi_{0})+\epsilon B, (6)

where the second term is non-negative and is positive whenever π0\pi_{0} induces non-zero median advantage. For a fixed π0\pi_{0}, we denote this constant improvement term as ϵ​B\epsilon B. A performance bound for general cases is provided in Theorem 4.2. Though π∗\pi^{*} is simple to express and provides improvement guarantees, it may not lie in the admissible policy class Π\Pi (Figure 2 Middle right). This motivates the design of policy optimization algorithms to minimize divergence between the policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and π∗\pi^{*}.

Revisiting the PPO loss function: We observe that the PPO loss function approximately drives the policy towards π∗\pi^{*} in (5). Specifically, as shown in Figure 3 (a-b), optimizing the PPO objective [23] is equivalent to minimizing the expectation of the following loss function evaluated at ρ=π⁡(a|s)/π0​(a|s)\rho=\pi(a|s)/\pi_{0}(a|s)

l′​(ρ):={|Aπ0|⋅|ρ−(1+ϵ⋅sign​(Aπ0))|,|ρ−1|≤ϵ,0,|ρ−1|>ϵ.\begin{split}&l^{\prime}(\rho):=\begin{cases}|A_{\pi_{0}}|\cdot|\rho-(1+\epsilon\cdot\text{sign}(A_{\pi_{0}}))|,&|\rho-1|\leq\epsilon,\\[2.0pt] 0,&|\rho-1|>\epsilon.\end{cases}\end{split} (7)

A formal theorem on this equivalence with step-by-step proof is detailed in Section 4.4 and Appendix A.5. At the beginning of the iteration, the ratio always starts from 1, and the PPO loss minimizes an advantage-weighted absolute error between the ratio ρ\rho and the target 1+ϵ​sign​(Aπ0)1+\epsilon\text{sign}(A_{\pi_{0}}), then it applies zero-gradient after reaching the target. Note that this target ratio closely matches the solution in (5), except that PPO uses the mean advantage Aπ0A_{\pi_{0}}, and the BRRL solution is expressed in terms of the median advantage A~π0\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}.

Bounded Policy Optimization (BPO): Building on the solution in (5), we introduce a natural PPO variant with the loss function lB​P​Ol^{BPO} to directly minimize the advantage weighted total variation from the optimal solution. For the solution in (5), the loss lB​P​Ol^{BPO} evaluated under ρ=π⁡(a|s)/π0​(a|s)\rho=\pi(a|s)/\pi_{0}(a|s) is

lB​P​O​(ρ):=|Aπ0|⋅|ρ−π∗​(a|s)π0​(a|s)|=|Aπ0|⋅|ρ−(1+ϵ⋅sign​(A~π0))|.l^{BPO}(\rho):=|A_{\pi_{0}}|\cdot\left|\rho-\frac{\pi^{*}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\right|=|A_{\pi_{0}}|\cdot|\rho-(1+\epsilon\cdot\text{sign}(\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}))|. (8)

The loss is illustrated in Figure 3 (d). Compared with the PPO loss in (7), this loss function l′l^{\prime} only differs in two ways: (1) a symmetric slope also for |ρ−1|≥ϵ|\rho-1|\geq\epsilon and (2) using A~π0\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}} instead of Aπ0A_{\pi_{0}}. In practice, this also requires learning an additional median value function alongside the mean value function, though the median can be approximated by the mean to reduce computational overhead. Notably, with this refined loss function, BPO has both theoretical performance guarantees (discussed below) and strong empirical performance, as demonstrated in Section 5. The same loss function can also be adapted for LLM fine-tuning, analogous to how PPO was adapted to GRPO (Section 4.5).

BPO performance guarantees: Assuming the optimal solution in (5) is valid, we can express the stepwise improvement in terms of the achieved loss (8). Specifically, we show that

η⁡(π)≥η⁡(π0)+ϵ​B−𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0​[lB​P​O​(π⁡(a|s)π0​(a|s))]−δ⁡(π,π∗),\displaystyle\eta(\pi)\geq\eta(\pi_{0})+\epsilon B-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}}\left[l^{BPO}\left(\frac{\pi(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\right)\right]-\delta(\pi,\pi^{*}),

where BB is defined in (6). Here, δ⁡(π,π∗)\delta(\pi,\pi^{*}) is an error term that is related to lB​P​O​(π⁡(a|s)π0​(a|s))l^{BPO}(\frac{\pi(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}) and reduces to 00 if we have perfect policy approximation π=π∗\pi=\pi^{*}. This theoretical result directly implies that, if our loss function lB​P​Ol^{BPO} is sufficiently minimized over states and actions sampled from π0\pi_{0}, and if the policy approximation error is small, we can obtain monotonic performance improvement. The formal result is detailed in Corollary 4.5.

4 Method

We now proceed to present the aforementioned framework of BRRL and its extensions.

4.1 Bounded Ratio RL Framework

Intuitively, for an MDP with finite state and action spaces, Problem (4) is a linear programming problem. Specifically, for a fixed state ss, the optimization variable π⁡(a|s)\pi(a|s) is a finite-dimensional vector. Consequently, the objective function and constraints in Problem (4) are linear in π⁡(a|s)\pi(a|s). However, for general state and action spaces, the optimal solution of this linear programming problem is difficult to specify analytically. Nevertheless, an additional regularizer allows for the derivation of the general analytical solution. Namely, we consider the following regularized constrained optimization problem:

maxπ⁡Lπ0​(π)−λ​𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0​[H⁡(π⁡(a|s)π0​(a|s))],whereH⁡(ρ):=(ρ−1+ϵ)​log⁡(ρ−1+ϵ)+(1+ϵ−ρ)​log⁡(1+ϵ−ρ).\begin{split}&\max_{\pi}\,L_{\pi_{0}}(\pi)-\lambda\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}}\left[H\left(\frac{\pi(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\right)\right],\\ \text{where}\quad&H(\rho):=(\rho-1+\epsilon)\log(\rho-1+\epsilon)+(1+\epsilon-\rho)\log(1+\epsilon-\rho).\end{split} (9)

Here the regularizer H⁡(ρ)∈[2​ϵ​log⁡ϵ,0)H(\rho)\in[2\epsilon\log\epsilon,0) decreases as ρ→1\rho\rightarrow 1 and increases as ρ→1±ϵ\rho\rightarrow 1\pm\epsilon. Moreover, its gradient becomes unbounded near the boundaries 1±ϵ1\pm\epsilon, so HH provides log barriers for the original bounded ratio constraints 1−ϵ<π⁡(a|s)π0​(a|s)<1+ϵ1-\epsilon<\frac{\pi(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}<1+\epsilon. The regularizer is weighted by λ\lambda. According to Fermi-Dirac statistics [10], Problem (9) has a closed-form solution, detailed in the following theorem.

Theorem 4.1 (Optimal solution).

The optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} of the problem described in (9) satisfies:

π∗​(a|s)=(1+ϵ​tanh⁡(A~π02​λ))​π0​(a|s),A~π0:=Qπ0​(s,a)−μπ0​(s),\displaystyle\pi^{*}(a|s)=\left(1+\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\right)\pi_{0}(a|s),\,\,\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}:=Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu_{\pi_{0}}(s),

where A~π0\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}} is the soft-median advantage and μπ0​(s)\mu_{\pi_{0}}(s) is the soft-median of Qπ0​(s,a)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a) that satisfies

𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[tanh(A~π02​λ)]=0⇔μπ0(s)=argminμ⁡(s)𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[g(Qπ0​(s,a)−μ​(s)λ)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\right]=0\,\,\Leftrightarrow\,\,\mu_{\pi_{0}}(s)=\arg\min_{\mu(s)}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[g\left(\frac{Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu(s)}{\lambda}\right)\right],

where g:ℝ→ℝ≥0,g⁡(x)=ln⁡(e−x2+ex2)g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},g(x)=\ln(e^{-\frac{x}{2}}+e^{\frac{x}{2}}) is a soft absolute function.

The detailed proof of Theorem 4.1 is provided in Appendix A.1. Intuitively, the optimal solution assigns a higher ratio to actions with a higher advantage while keeping the ratio between [1−ϵ,1+ϵ][1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon].

We can obtain a monotonic performance guarantee for the optimal solution.

Theorem 4.2 (Monotonic performance guarantee).

The optimal policy in Theorem 4.1 satisfies

η(π∗)≥η(π0)+ϵ𝔼s∼dπ∗,a∼π0(⋅|s)[tanh(A~π02​λ)A~π0]=:η(π0)+ϵB,\displaystyle\eta(\pi^{*})\geq\eta(\pi_{0})+\epsilon\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi^{*}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}\right]=:\eta(\pi_{0})+\epsilon B,

where A~π0\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}} abbreviates A~π0​(s,a)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a), BB is a non-negative constant given fixed π0\pi_{0}.

The proof of Theorem 4.2 is detailed in Appendix A.2. Note that the term tanh⁡(A~π02​λ)​A~π0\tanh(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda})\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}} is always non-negative since the signs of tanh⁡(A~π02​λ)\tanh(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}) and A~π0\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}} are always the same. Therefore, our optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} guarantees monotonic improvement with an analytical improvement bound, in contrast to the guarantee for TRPO in Theorem 1 of [21]. However, the policy π∗\pi^{*} may not be a member of the class of parameterized policies Π\Pi. Consequently, in Section 4.2 and 4.3, we further develop the policy optimization loss algorithm by minimizing a certain divergence from π\pi to π∗\pi^{*}.

Remark 4.3 (Optimal solution to unregularized Problem (4)).

Note that by taking λ→0\lambda\rightarrow 0 in Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.2, one can obtain the optimal ratio and monotonic guarantees for the unregularized Problem (4). In many cases, one can simplify the resulting optimal policy as π∗​(a|s)=[1+ϵ​sign​(A~π0)]​π0​(a|s)\pi^{*}(a|s)=[1+\epsilon\text{sign}(\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}})]\pi_{0}(a|s) in (5), where μπ0​(s)\mu_{\pi_{0}}(s) is the median of Qπ0​(s,a)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a) over π0(⋅|s)\pi_{0}(\cdot|s). Such simplification holds if ∀s,∃μ⁡(s)\forall\,s,\,\exists\,\mu(s), such that

𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[sign(Qπ0(s,a)−μ(s))]=0.\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\text{sign}(Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu(s))]=0. (10)

Otherwise, the simplified π∗\pi^{*} can never be normalized. One valid case is a uniform density π0(⋅|s)\pi_{0}(\cdot|s) with continuous 𝒜\mathcal{A} and a QQ-function Qπ0​(s,a)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a) which is smooth over aa. However, there are also counterexamples. Consider, for instance, an MDP with a single state and a discrete action space 𝒜={a1,a2}.\mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},a_{2}\}. Assume that Qπ0​(a2)>Qπ0​(a1)Q_{\pi_{0}}(a_{2})>Q_{\pi_{0}}(a_{1}), and π0​(a1)=14,π0​(a2)=34\pi_{0}(a_{1})=\frac{1}{4},\pi_{0}(a_{2})=\frac{3}{4}. Then for any μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R}, condition (10) does not hold. While the simplified interpretation of π∗\pi^{*} is only valid in special cases, the result of Theorem 4.1 still holds for arbitrarily small λ>0\lambda>0 and general spaces (see Appendix A.1).

4.2 Alternative Perspective: Minimizing Divergence from Optimal Policy

In this section, we consider the policy optimization problem as minimizing the divergence to the optimal solution, instead of directly applying policy gradient methods. Specifically, given the optimal policy obtained from Theorem 4.1, we can formulate policy optimization as

minπθ∈Π⁡D⁡(πθ,π∗),\displaystyle\min_{\pi_{\theta}\in\Pi}D(\pi_{\theta},\pi^{*}),

where πθ\pi_{\theta} is the parameterized policy, DD is a divergence function such as the KL-divergence, total variation (TV), etc. Specifically, the TV for each state can be expressed as

DθT​V(s):=∑a|π∗(a|s)−πθ(a|s)|=𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[|π∗​(a|s)π0​(a|s)−πθ​(a|s)π0​(a|s)|].\begin{split}D_{\theta}^{TV}(s):=\sum_{a}\left|\pi^{*}(a|s)-\pi_{\theta}(a|s)\right|=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\left|\frac{\pi^{*}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}-\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\right|\right].\end{split} (11)

We also consider an advantage-weighted TV (ATV) loss function defined as

DθA​T​V(s):=𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[|π∗​(a|s)π0​(a|s)−πθ​(a|s)π0​(a|s)|⋅|Aπ0|].\begin{split}&D_{\theta}^{ATV}(s):=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\left|\frac{\pi^{*}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}-\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\right|\cdot\left|A_{\pi_{0}}\right|\right].\end{split} (12)

Notably, this divergence is directly correlated with the performance improvement of the parameterized policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, as detailed in the following Corollary.

Corollary 4.4 (Performance improvement guarantee with policy approximation error).

Consider DθA​T​VD_{\theta}^{ATV} defined in (12) with π∗\pi^{*} given from Theorem 4.1. Then it holds that

η(πθ)≥η(π0)+𝔼s∼dπθ,a∼π0(⋅|s)[ϵtanh(A~π02​λ)A~π0−DθA​T​V(s)],\displaystyle\eta(\pi_{\theta})\geq\eta(\pi_{0})+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim{d_{\pi_{\theta}},a\sim\pi_{0}}(\cdot|s)}\left[\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}-D_{\theta}^{ATV}(s)\right],

where A~π0\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}} abbreviates A~π0​(s,a)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a).

The proof of Corollary 4.4 is provided in A.3. Corollary 4.4 shows that by minimizing the loss DθA​T​VD_{\theta}^{ATV} over the state distribution dπθd_{\pi_{\theta}}, we can improve performance w.r.t. policy πθ\pi_{\theta} as long as the parameterized policy class is sufficiently expressive. However, minimizing 𝔼s∼dπθ\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{\theta}}} over the policy parameters θ\theta is non-trivial due to the dependence of the state distribution on πθ\pi_{\theta}. Consequently, in practice we only optimize the expectation of the divergence over the old policy, leading to the objectives

JA​T​V​(θ):=𝔼s∼dπ0​[DθA​T​V​(s)],JT​V​(θ):=𝔼s∼dπ0​[DθT​V​(s)].J^{ATV}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}}}[D_{\theta}^{ATV}(s)],\quad J^{TV}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}}}[D_{\theta}^{TV}(s)]. (13)

The following Corollary 4.5 expresses a lower bound on the performance of the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} in terms of these quantities.

Corollary 4.5 (Performance improvement guarantee with loss functions).

With BB defined in Theorem 4.2, and δ~:=maxs𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[tanh(A~π02​λ)A~π0]\tilde{\delta}:=\max_{s}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}\right], it holds that

η⁡(πθ)≥\displaystyle\eta(\pi_{\theta})\geq\,\, η⁡(π0)+ϵ​B−JA​T​V​(θ)−DmaxA​T​V1−γ​JT​V​(θ)−γ​ϵ​DmaxA​T​V(1−γ)2−γ​ϵ​δ~​DmaxT​V(1−γ)2,\displaystyle\eta(\pi_{0})+\epsilon B-J^{ATV}(\theta)-\frac{D^{ATV}_{\max}}{1-\gamma}J^{TV}(\theta)-\frac{\gamma\epsilon D^{ATV}_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}-\frac{\gamma\epsilon\tilde{\delta}D^{TV}_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}},

where DmaxA​T​V:=maxs⁡DθA​T​V​(s)D^{ATV}_{\max}:=\max_{s}D_{\theta}^{ATV}(s) and DmaxT​V:=maxs⁡DθT​V​(s)D^{TV}_{\max}:=\max_{s}D_{\theta}^{TV}(s).

The proof of Corollary 4.5 is detailed in Appendix A.4. Corollary 4.5 decomposes the performance lower bound into a non-negative term, ϵ​B\epsilon B, and several negative terms which depend on the gap between the optimized policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and the policy π∗\pi^{*}. The first two of these gap terms depend on JA​T​V​(θ)J^{ATV}(\theta) and JT​V​(θ)J^{TV}(\theta). Both of these quantities can be estimated from trajectories collected under π0\pi_{0} and minimized by optimizing θ\theta, motivating a loss defined as a weighted combination of these terms. The other two gap terms are characterized by the worst case divergence of πθ\pi_{\theta} from π∗\pi^{*} over the state space through the quantities DmaxA​T​VD_{\max}^{ATV} and DmaxT​VD_{\max}^{TV}. Though these quantities are generally not computable, they can be related to the expected losses over the distribution dπ0d_{\pi_{0}} under additional assumptions (e.g., adequate state coverage under dπ0d_{\pi_{0}}). Notably, with perfect policy approximation (OPENπθ=π∗)\pi_{\theta}=\pi^{*}), it holds that JA​T​V​(θ)=JT​V​(θ)=DmaxA​T​V=DmaxT​V=0,J^{ATV}(\theta)=J^{TV}(\theta)=D^{ATV}_{\max}=D^{TV}_{\max}=0, recovering the original monotonic performance guarantee of Theorem 4.2.

In contrast, the bound from TRPO in Theorem 1 of [21] does not contain a positive term. Besides, it penalizes the worst-case divergence between the updated policy and the current policy π0\pi_{0} through DT​Vmax​(π,π0)D_{TV}^{\max}(\pi,\pi_{0}), rather than the approximation error to an ideal solution π∗\pi^{*}. Consequently, this negative term reflects the magnitude of the update away from π0\pi_{0}. It vanishes only in the degenerate case π=π0\pi=\pi_{0} (i.e., no policy change), and is generally nonzero whenever a nontrivial policy update occurs.

Corollary 4.5 also motivates choosing a small ϵ\epsilon. For small ϵ>0\epsilon>0, π∗\pi^{*} remains close to π0\pi_{0} by construction, so matching π∗\pi^{*} typically requires only a small deviation from a realizable policy in the class (namely π0\pi_{0}), making the approximation error terms easier to control. Since π0\pi_{0} is realizable in the policy class, the optimal values of JA​T​V​(θ)J^{ATV}(\theta) and JT​V​(θ)J^{TV}(\theta) approach zero as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0. Therefore, under such regularity conditions, it holds that γ​DmaxA​T​V(1−γ)2+γ​δ~​DmaxT​V(1−γ)2≪B\frac{\gamma D_{\max}^{ATV}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}+\frac{\gamma\tilde{\delta}D_{\max}^{TV}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\ll B for ϵ\epsilon sufficiently small, therefore guaranteeing improvement.

4.3 Bounded Policy Optimization

In this section, we present the practical implementation of our algorithm. As in PPO, we use a value network VϕV_{\phi} to estimate Aπ0A_{\pi_{0}}. Specifically, we estimate the return value Rϕ​(s,a)R_{\phi}(s,a) using generalized advantage estimation [22], and use it to update the value function by minimizing

JV​F(ϕ):=𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[(Rϕ(s,a)−Vϕ(s))2].\displaystyle J^{VF}(\phi):=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[(R_{\phi}(s,a)-V_{\phi}(s))^{2}]. (14)

In addition, following Theorem 4.1, we further train a network μψ\mu_{\psi} to minimize the normalization loss

JM​F(ψ):=𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[λg(Rϕ​(s,a)−μψ​(s)λ)].\displaystyle J^{MF}(\psi):=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\lambda g\left(\frac{R_{\phi}(s,a)-\mu_{\psi}(s)}{\lambda}\right)\right]. (15)

The practical loss function for θ\theta uses the estimated advantage function to approximate JP​(θ):=JA​T​V​(θ)+α1​JT​V​(θ)J^{P}(\theta):=J^{ATV}(\theta)+\alpha_{1}J^{TV}(\theta) with α1\alpha_{1} as a tunable weight:

J^P(θ):=𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[|1+ϵtanh(A^π02​λ)−πθ​(a|s)π0​(a|s)|⋅(|Rϕ(s,a)−Vϕ(s)|+α1)],\begin{split}\hat{J}^{P}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\left|1+\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\hat{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)-\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\right|\cdot\left(\left|R_{\phi}(s,a)-V_{\phi}(s)\right|+\alpha_{1}\right)\right],\end{split} (16)

where A^π0:=Rϕ​(s,a)−μψ​(s)\hat{A}_{\pi_{0}}:=R_{\phi}(s,a)-\mu_{\psi}(s). Note that J^P​(θ)\hat{J}^{P}(\theta) is not exactly JPJ^{P}, but the gap can be controlled by minimizing the estimation error of VϕV_{\phi} and μψ\mu_{\psi}. Our final bounded policy optimization algorithm follows a PPO-style training procedure, summarized in Algorithm 1.

4.4 Revisiting the PPO Objective

In this section, we connect our theory and algorithmic framework to PPO [23]. In PPO, the following surrogate objective function is introduced

𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0​[min⁡{clip​(ρ,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​Aπ0,ρ​Aπ0}]:=JP​P​O​(θ),\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}}\left[\min\left\{\text{clip}\left(\rho,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)A_{\pi_{0}},\rho A_{\pi_{0}}\right\}\right]:=J_{PPO}(\theta), (17)

where ρ:=πθ​(a|s)π0​(a|s)\rho:=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)} is the ratio between the new and old policies, and Aπ0A_{\pi_{0}} denotes Aπ0​(s,a)A_{\pi_{0}}(s,a).

We observe a strong correlation between the BPO loss function and the PPO loss function. To show this correlation, we first introduce an equivalent form of the PPO loss in the following proposition.

Proposition 4.6.

Optimizing the loss function JP​P​O​(θ)J_{PPO}(\theta) in (17) is equivalent to minimizing the following function

J′(θ):=𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[l′(πθ​(a|s)π0​(a|s))],\displaystyle J^{\prime}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim{d_{\pi_{0}}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[l^{\prime}\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\right)\right],

where

l′​(ρ):={|Aπ0|⋅|ρ−(1+ϵ⋅sign​(Aπ0))|,|ρ−1|≤ϵ,0,|ρ−1|>ϵ.\displaystyle l^{\prime}(\rho):=\begin{cases}|A_{\pi_{0}}|\cdot|\rho-(1+\epsilon\cdot\text{sign}(A_{\pi_{0}}))|,&|\rho-1|\leq\epsilon,\\[2.0pt] 0,&|\rho-1|>\epsilon.\end{cases}

Intuitively, this equivalence follows from the fact that adding or subtracting a constant from the objective function does not change the optimal solution. This is illustrated in Fig. 3 (a vs b). A proof is provided in Appendix A.5.

On the other hand, as λ→0\lambda\to 0, the loss JA​T​VJ^{ATV} in (13) can, in many cases (Remark 4.3), be expressed as

JA​T​V(θ)≈𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π(⋅|s)[lB​P​O(ρ)],wherelB​P​O(ρ)=|Aπ0|⋅|ρ−(1+ϵ⋅sign(A~π0))|.\displaystyle J^{ATV}(\theta)\approx\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}[l^{BPO}(\rho)],\quad\text{where}\,\,l^{BPO}(\rho)=|A_{\pi_{0}}|\cdot|\rho-(1+\epsilon\cdot\text{sign}(\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}))|.

Thus, the loss lB​P​Ol^{BPO} resembles the PPO loss l′l^{\prime} in Proposition 4.6 when |ρ−1|≤ϵ|\rho-1|\leq\epsilon, as detailed in Section 2. For |ρ−1|>ϵ|\rho-1|>\epsilon, BPO penalizes the policy for deviating from the original policy, which encourages satisfaction of the bounded-ratio constraints. This is also partially addressed by the zero gradient of PPO and the target KL divergence mechanism (25), which slows down the update of the new policy if it deviates too far from the original policy (i.e., if the KL divergence between the two surpasses the target KL divergence). Recent PPO variants also utilize similar ideas by introducing negative gradients when |ρ−1|>ϵ|\rho-1|>\epsilon [30, 33], which can be theoretically justified by our framework. Although the exact optimization dynamics of BPO and PPO differ, both follow a common principle: drive the policy ratio from 11 toward the (approximate) analytical optimum of BRRL and then stop. This offers a key insight into the underlying success of PPO-based methods.

4.5 Extension to LLM Fine-Tuning

In the context of LLM fine-tuning, training an additional critic can be computationally expensive. This challenge motivates the design of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [26], which estimates advantages relative to a group of concurrent samples rather than utilizing an auxiliary value network. Building on this idea, we introduce Group-relative Bounded Policy Optimization (GBPO), an extension of BPO derived from Theorem 4.1. Specifically, for a given prompt qq, the model generates a group of sampled outcomes {o1,o2,…,oG}\{o_{1},o_{2},\dots,o_{G}\}. A reward model then assigns a score to each output, denoted by 𝐑={r1,r2,…,rG}\mathbf{R}=\{r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{G}\}. As in standard GRPO, we estimate advantages using z-scores Ai:=ri−mean​(𝐑)std​(𝐑)A_{i}:=\frac{r_{i}-\text{mean}(\mathbf{R})}{\text{std}(\mathbf{R})}. As noted in Remark 4.3, when the regularization parameter λ\lambda is small, the implicit baseline μπ0​(q)\mu_{\pi_{0}}(q) converges to the median of the Q-values. We therefore also estimate the median-advantage as A~i:=ri−median​(𝐑)std​(𝐑)\tilde{A}_{i}:=\frac{r_{i}-\text{median}(\mathbf{R})}{\text{std}(\mathbf{R})}. The GBPO objective function is then defined as:

J^P​(θ)=𝔼q∼P⁡(𝒬)oi∼π0(⋅|q)​[1G​∑i=1G1|oi|​∑t=1|oi||1+ϵ​tanh⁡(A~i2​λ)−πθ​(oi,t|q,oi,<t)π0​(oi,t|q,oi,<t)|⋅|Ai,t|],\displaystyle\hat{J}^{P}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim P(\mathcal{Q})\\ o_{i}\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|q)\end{subarray}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|o_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}\left|1+\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{i}}{2\lambda}\right)-\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{0}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})}\right|\cdot|A_{i,t}|\Bigg],

where tt denotes the token index, and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is the question set. In scenarios where a reward is only provided at the end of the sequence, the step-dependent advantages Ai,tA_{i,t} and A~i,t\tilde{A}_{i,t} are equal to the sequence-level AiA_{i} and A~i\tilde{A}_{i}, respectively. If per-step scores are available, these advantages can be estimated token-wise following the approach in [26].

4.6 Asymmetric Ratio Constraints and Cross Entropy Method

In this section, we generalize Theorem 4.1 to asymmetric ratio constraints. Similar to (9), we consider the regularized problem with general ratio boundaries ∀s,a,cl≤π⁡(a|s)π0​(a|s)≤ch\forall s,a,\,\,c_{l}\leq\frac{\pi(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\leq c_{h}, with cl<1<chc_{l}<1<c_{h}

maxπ⁡Lπ0​(π)−λ​𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0​[H′​(π⁡(a|s)π0​(a|s))],whereH′​(ρ):=(ρ−cl)​log⁡(ρ−cl)+(ch−ρ)​log⁡(ch−ρ)+log⁡ch−11−cl​ρ.\begin{split}&\max_{\pi}\,L_{\pi_{0}}(\pi)-\lambda\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}}\left[H^{\prime}\left(\frac{\pi(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}\right)\right],\\ \text{where}\quad&H^{\prime}(\rho):=(\rho-c_{l})\log(\rho-c_{l})+(c_{h}-\rho)\log(c_{h}-\rho)+\log\frac{c_{h}-1}{1-c_{l}}\rho.\end{split} (18)

Here, the regularizer H′H^{\prime} still takes its maximum at ρ=1\rho=1, and provides log barriers for the asymmetric constraints cl≤ρ≤chc_{l}\leq\rho\leq c_{h}. The optimal solution is detailed in the following Corollary.

Corollary 4.7.

(Asymmetric optimal policy) The optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} of the problem (18) satisfies

π∗​(a|s)π0​(a|s)=cl+ch−cl1+ch−11−clexp(−A~′π0/λ),A~π0′:=Qπ0​(s,a)−μπ0′​(s),\displaystyle\frac{\pi^{*}(a|s)}{\pi_{0}(a|s)}=c_{l}+\frac{c_{h}-c_{l}}{1+\frac{c_{h}-1}{1-c_{l}}\exp(-\tilde{A}^{\prime}_{\pi_{0}}/{\lambda})},\,\,\tilde{A}^{\prime}_{\pi_{0}}:=Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu^{\prime}_{\pi_{0}}(s),

where μπ0′​(s)\mu^{\prime}_{\pi_{0}}(s) is the soft-ch−1ch−cl\frac{c_{h}-1}{c_{h}-c_{l}}-quantile satisfying

μπ0′(s)=argminμ⁡(s)𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[g′(Qπ0​(s,a)−μ​(s)λ)],\displaystyle\mu^{\prime}_{\pi_{0}}(s)=\arg\min_{\mu(s)}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[g^{\prime}\left(\frac{Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu(s)}{\lambda}\right)\right],

where g′:ℝ→ℝ≥0,g′​(x)=ln⁡(ech−1ch−cl​x+ch−11−cl​e−1−clch−cl​x)g^{\prime}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},g^{\prime}(x)=\ln\left(e^{\frac{c_{h}-1}{c_{h}-c_{l}}x}+\frac{c_{h}-1}{1-c_{l}}e^{-\frac{1-c_{l}}{c_{h}-c_{l}}x}\right).

Similar to Theorem 4.1, these results are closely related to policy optimization with asymmetric clip ratios [29, 32]. A monotonic performance guarantee similar to Theorem 4.2 is provided in Appendix A.7. Moreover, when λ→0\lambda\rightarrow 0, we also have μπ0′​(s)\mu^{\prime}_{\pi_{0}}(s) the exact ch−1ch−cl\frac{c_{h}-1}{c_{h}-c_{l}}-quantile in many cases, similar to Remark 4.3. Notably, when cl=0c_{l}=0, λ→0\lambda\rightarrow 0, and the ch−1ch−cl\frac{c_{h}-1}{c_{h}-c_{l}}-quantile exists for Qπ0​(s,a)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a), we have π∗​(a|s)=ch​π0​(a|s)\pi^{*}(a|s)=c_{h}\pi_{0}(a|s) for Qπ0​(s,a)>μπ0′​(s)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)>\mu^{\prime}_{\pi_{0}}(s) and 00 otherwise. This recovers a cross-entropy method (CEM) when π0\pi_{0} is uniform, where the optimal solution at each iteration assigns non-zero probability to the top 1−clch−cl\frac{1-c_{l}}{c_{h}-c_{l}} samples.

5 Experiments

In this section, we present extensive experiments to validate the proposed BPO algorithm. We first benchmark its performance against PPO across standard MuJoCo and Atari environments (Section 5.1). To assess scalability, we evaluate BPO within NVIDIA IsaacLab [15], a high-throughput simulation platform capable of simulating thousands of parallel environments for real-world robotic policy training. Furthermore, we apply our GBPO variant to LLM fine-tuning tasks, and compare it directly against GRPO (Section 5.3). Then, we dive deeper into the analysis of the ratio statistics during training, connecting it to the performance gap between BPO and PPO. Finally, we conduct an ablation study to analyze the sensitivity of training performance to key components, including the loss function, the λ\lambda parameter, and various loss coefficients. All hyperparameters are detailed in Appendix A.8

5.1 Benchmarking with Classical Environments

We compare the performance of BPO and PPO in classical environments. For these experiments, BPO was implemented within the Stable Baselines3 framework, with hyperparameters for all baseline algorithms sourced from RL-Zoo [20]. As shown in Figure 4, BPO performs competitively with or superior to PPO across a range of classical benchmarks. Specifically, in MuJoCo tasks, BPO achieves clear performance gains in the Ant-v4, Hopper-v4, and Humanoid-v4 environments. Training on Humanoid-v4 exhibits high variance for BPO, characterized by significant performance divergence across random seeds. Both PPO and BPO struggle to achieve peak performance in this environment, primarily due to limited sample efficiency. However, as demonstrated in Section 5.2, both methods successfully solve more complex humanoid tasks when provided with sufficient samples. In Atari benchmarks, BPO generally matches PPO’s performance, notably outperforming it in the Asterix environment.

We report our benchmarking results against off-policy baselines in MuJoCo and Atari environments in Table 1. While SAC [7] outperforms both PPO and BPO in the Ant-v4 and Humanoid-v4 tasks, it fails to achieve competitive results in Swimmer-v4. In contrast, BPO consistently outperforms PPO in the Ant-v4, Humanoid-v4, and Hopper-v4 environments while remaining competitive in Swimmer-v4. Both BPO and PPO consistently outperform DQN [16] in Atari benchmarks.

5.2 Benchmarking with IsaacLab Environments

In this section, we evaluate the scalability and performance of BPO relative to PPO within the IsaacLab simulation platform. We focus on four challenging locomotion tasks on rough terrain: Go1-rough, Anymal-C-rough, G1-rough, and H1-rough, which require the agents (quadrupeds like Unitree Go1 and Anymal-C or humanoids like Unitree G1 and H1) to maintain stable gaits while tracking target velocities across rough surfaces. Both BPO and PPO were implemented using the RSL-RL framework, utilizing a large-scale parallelization of 4,096 environments per task.

The results in Figure 5 demonstrate that BPO is highly effective in complex robotic locomotion tasks. In particular, on G1-rough, BPO significantly outperforms the baseline to reach a higher performance ceiling. For the Go1-rough and H1-rough environment, BPO also slightly exceeds the final performance of PPO. Notably, across all four benchmarks, BPO exhibits enhanced training stability and smoother dynamics compared to the PPO baseline.

5.3 LLM Fine-Tuning with GBPO

We further evaluate GBPO against GRPO for large language model fine-tuning (Section 4.5). Specifically, we conduct experiments in the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL, [35]) framework, fine-tuning the Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B model with GBPO and GRPO on the AIME-TTT and AMC-TTT benchmarks, and then compare their reasoning performance. The empirical results, illustrated in Figure 6, reveal that GBPO can maintain performance gains as the number of training epochs and clip ratio increase. Conversely, GRPO exhibits instability under these conditions. These findings highlight GBPO’s potential as a more robust and stable alternative for the fine-tuning of large-scale models.

5.4 Ratio Statistics Analysis

We analyze the statistics of importance weights (ratio π⁡(a|s)/π0​(a|s)\pi(a|s)/\pi_{0}(a|s)) during the training process. In MuJoCo environments (using the stable-baselines3 implementation), BPO maintains more stable ratio distributions than PPO, as illustrated in Figure 7. This difference in stability is more obvious in environments where BPO outperforms PPO (e.g., Hopper and Asterix).

In IsaacLab environments (utilizing RSL-RL), learning rates are dynamically adjusted to maintain a target KL divergence. As shown in Figure 8, the adapted learning rates for PPO are often lower than those for BPO, suggesting more aggressive ratio updates that surpass the target KL divergence more frequently. The scales of the learning rates differ more in tasks where BPO shows a clear performance improvement (e.g., G1-rough). These findings suggest a strong correlation between the stability of ratio distributions and overall algorithmic performance. By effectively enforcing this stability, BPO allows for more stable performance improvement.

5.5 Ablation Study

This section presents an ablation study of the impact of the value function, loss function, λ\lambda, and the coefficient of TV loss on the performance of the policy, within the G1-rough environment.

Mean vs median value function. We evaluate the performance of the algorithm by substituting median advantages A~π0\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}} with the mean advantage Aπ0{A}_{\pi_{0}}. As illustrated in the left panel of Figure 9, this simplification achieves performance comparable to the original BPO. This robustness likely stems from the low practical differences between median and mean values, caused by the specific return distribution and inherent value estimation errors. These results also suggest that this median-to-mean value simplification offers a compelling alternative when the computational overhead of learning the median value is high.

Divergence function ablation. As illustrated in the middle-left panel of Figure 9, the ATV loss consistently yields superior performance in both G1-rough and Anymal-C-rough environments. While the standard TV loss facilitates some learning, it fails to match the asymptotic performance of ATV. Conversely, KL divergence proves ineffective and fails to achieve successful policy convergence.

Sensitivity to λ\lambda. We conduct a hyperparameter sweep for λ\lambda in the G1-rough environment. As shown in the middle-right panel of Figure 9 , smaller values of λ\lambda generally lead to strong performance. Specifically, increasing λ\lambda from 10−310^{-3} to 10−210^{-2} may slightly improve asymptotic performance, but at the cost of a reduced convergence rate. Conversely, excessively large values of λ\lambda prevent the learning process entirely.

Impact of TV loss regularization. We study the effect of the TV loss coefficient by incrementally increasing its weight relative to the ATV loss in the G1-rough environment. Although Corollary 4.5 suggests that both terms contribute to performance gains, the results in the right panel of Figure 9 indicate that explicitly adding a TV loss component does not improve performance in practice.

6 Conclusion

We introduced Bounded Ratio Reinforcement Learning (BRRL), a framework for policy optimization under bounded ratio constraints. We showed that the underlying optimization problem admits an analytic solution. Our main finding is that this optimal solution allows interpreting the PPO loss from a new perspective, connects to the cross-entropy method (CEM), and motivates a theoretically grounded variant, Bounded Policy Optimization (BPO). Empirically, BPO is consistently effective across a broad range of tasks, including robotic control and large-model fine-tuning. Despite the extensive evaluation with standard RL benchmarks, extending the experiments towards a broader range of LLM fine-tuning tasks remains a compelling future direction. Other future research directions include enhancing sample efficiency via advanced exploration, extending the framework to constrained MDPs, and adapting the algorithm for fine-tuning generative policies.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Proof of Theorem 4.1

Proof.

Since ∀s,𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρ]=1\forall\,s,\,\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho]=1, we have from Equation (3)

Lπ0(π)=η(π0)+𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρAπ0(s,a)]\displaystyle L_{\pi_{0}}(\pi)=\eta(\pi_{0})+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho A_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼s∼dπ0[Vπ0(s)⋅𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρ]]+𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρAπ0(s,a)]\displaystyle\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}}}[V_{\pi_{0}}(s)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho]]+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho A_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρVπ0(s)+ρAπ0(s,a)]=𝔼s∼dπ0,a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρQπ0(s,a)]\displaystyle\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho V_{\pi_{0}}(s)+\rho A_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)]=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi_{0}},a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)]

The original problem (9) can then be written as

maxρ⁡𝔼s∼dπ0a∼π0(⋅|s)​[ρ​Qπ0​(s,a)−λ⁡(ρ−1+ϵ)​log⁡(ρ−1+ϵ)−λ⁡(1+ϵ−ρ)​log⁡(1+ϵ−ρ)],\displaystyle\max_{\rho}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\sim d_{\pi_{0}}\\ a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)\end{subarray}}[\rho Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\lambda(\rho-1+\epsilon)\log(\rho-1+\epsilon)-\lambda(1+\epsilon-\rho)\log(1+\epsilon-\rho)],

with the normalization constraint

∀s,𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρ]=1.\displaystyle\forall\,s,\,\,\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho]=1.

This optimization problem can be decomposed into subproblems for each state ss. Now, given a fixed state ss, we solve the constrained optimization problem using the Lagrangian approach, with a Lagrangian multiplier denoted as −μ⁡(s)-\mu(s)

ℒ⁡(ρ):=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\rho):= 𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρQπ0(s,a)−λ(ρ−1+ϵ)log(ρ−1+ϵ)−λ(1+ϵ−ρ)log(1+ϵ−ρ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{a\sim{\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}}[\rho Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\lambda(\rho-1+\epsilon)\log(\rho-1+\epsilon)-\lambda(1+\epsilon-\rho)\log(1+\epsilon-\rho)]
−μ(s)(𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[ρ]−1)\displaystyle-\mu(s)(\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}[\rho]-1)
=:\displaystyle=: 𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[f(ρ)]+μ(s),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{a\sim{\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}}[f(\rho)]+\mu(s),

where

f⁡(ρ):=ρ​Qπ0​(s,a)−λ⁡(ρ−1+ϵ)​log⁡(ρ−1+ϵ)−λ⁡(1+ϵ−ρ)​log⁡(1+ϵ−ρ)−μ⁡(s)​ρ.\displaystyle f(\rho):=\rho Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\lambda(\rho-1+\epsilon)\log(\rho-1+\epsilon)-\lambda(1+\epsilon-\rho)\log(1+\epsilon-\rho)-\mu(s)\rho.

If 𝒜\mathcal{A} is continuous, we apply the calculus of variations

∂∂ρ​f​(ρ)=0⇒∂∂ρ​(ρ​Qπ0​(s,a)−λ⁡(ρ−1+ϵ)​log⁡(ρ−1+ϵ)−λ⁡(1+ϵ−ρ)​log⁡(1+ϵ−ρ)−μ⁡(s)​ρ)=0⇒Qπ0​(s,a)−λ⁡(log⁡(ρ−1+ϵ)−log⁡(1+ϵ−ρ))−μ⁡(s)=0⇒log⁡ρ−1+ϵ1+ϵ−ρ=Qπ0​(s,a)−μ​(s)λ⇒ρ∗=1+ϵ​exp⁡(Qπ0​(s,a)−μ​(s)λ)−ϵ1+exp⁡(Qπ0​(s,a)−μ​(s)λ)=1+ϵ​tanh⁡(A~π02​λ)\begin{split}&\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}f(\rho)=0\\ \Rightarrow\quad&\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\left(\rho Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\lambda(\rho-1+\epsilon)\log(\rho-1+\epsilon)-\lambda(1+\epsilon-\rho)\log(1+\epsilon-\rho)-\mu(s)\rho\right)=0\\ \Rightarrow\quad&Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\lambda(\log(\rho-1+\epsilon)-\log(1+\epsilon-\rho))-\mu(s)=0\\ \Rightarrow\quad&\log\frac{\rho-1+\epsilon}{1+\epsilon-\rho}=\frac{Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu(s)}{\lambda}\\ \Rightarrow\quad&\rho^{*}=1+\frac{\epsilon\exp\left(\frac{Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu(s)}{\lambda}\right)-\epsilon}{1+\exp\left(\frac{Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu(s)}{\lambda}\right)}=1+\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\end{split} (19)

The second derivative of the objective function can be computed as −λρ−1+ϵ−λ1+ϵ−ρ-\frac{\lambda}{\rho-1+\epsilon}-\frac{\lambda}{1+\epsilon-\rho}, which is negative for arbitrary 1−ϵ<ρ<1+ϵ1-\epsilon<\rho<1+\epsilon. Therefore, ρ∗\rho^{*} is the maximizer of the objective function.

The Lagrangian multiplier μ⁡(s)\mu(s) should be chosen to satisfy the normalization constraint:

𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[1+ϵtanh(A~π02​λ)]=1⇔𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[tanh(A~π02​λ)]=0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[1+\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\right]=1\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\right]=0.

Note that such μ⁡(s)\mu(s) always exists because for all λ>0\lambda>0, 𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[1+ϵtanh(A~π02​λ)]\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[1+\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\right] is a smooth function of μ\mu with the value range between 1−ϵ1-\epsilon and 1+ϵ1+\epsilon. Now we show that the corresponding μ⁡(s)\mu(s) is also the minimizer of 𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[g(Qπ0​(s,a)−μ​(s)λ)]\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[g\left(\frac{Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\mu(s)}{\lambda}\right)\right], where g:=ln⁡(e−x2+ex2)g:=\ln(e^{-\frac{x}{2}}+e^{\frac{x}{2}}):

𝔼π0​[∂g∂u​(q−uλ)]=0⇔𝔼π0​[eq−u2​λ−e−q−u2​λ2​(e−q−u2​λ+eq−u2​λ)]=0⇔𝔼π0​[tanh⁡(q−u2​λ)]=0,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\frac{\partial g}{\partial u}\left(\frac{q-u}{\lambda}\right)\right]=0\,\,\Leftrightarrow\,\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\frac{e^{\frac{q-u}{2\lambda}}-e^{-\frac{q-u}{2\lambda}}}{2(e^{-\frac{q-u}{2\lambda}}+e^{\frac{q-u}{2\lambda}})}\right]=0\,\,\Leftrightarrow\,\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{q-u}{2\lambda}\right)\right]=0,

where 𝔼π0\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}} abbreviates 𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}. Besides,

∂2g∂2u=14​λ2𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[(eu−q2​λ+e−u−q2​λ)2−(eu−q2​λ−e−u−q2​λ)22​(e−u−q2​λ+eu−q2​λ)2]≥0.\frac{\partial^{2}g}{\partial^{2}u}=\frac{1}{4\lambda^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\frac{(e^{\frac{u-q}{2\lambda}}+e^{-\frac{u-q}{2\lambda}})^{2}-(e^{\frac{u-q}{2\lambda}}-e^{-\frac{u-q}{2\lambda}})^{2}}{2(e^{-\frac{u-q}{2\lambda}}+e^{\frac{u-q}{2\lambda}})^{2}}\right]\geq 0.

Therefore, the optimal μ⁡(s)\mu(s) is the minimizer of gg.

If 𝒜\mathcal{A} is discrete, for each fixed state ss, we denote the vectorized ρ⁡(a)\rho(a), Qπ0​(s,a)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a), H⁡(ρ)H(\rho) and π0​(a|s)\pi_{0}(a|s) as ρ,Q,H,π∈ℝ|𝒜|\rho,Q,H,\pi\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|}. Then the Lagrangian ℒ⁡(ρ)\mathcal{L}(\rho) can be expressed by

ℒ⁡(ρ):=π⊤​(ρ⊙Q−λ​H−μ​ρ)+μ,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\rho):=\pi^{\top}(\rho\odot Q-\lambda H-\mu\rho)+\mu,

where ⊙\odot denotes elementwise product. Applying zero gradient w.r.t. ρ\rho gives

(diag​(Q)−λ​diag​(H′)−μ​I)⊤​π=𝟎⇒π⁡(a|s)​(Qπ0​(s,a)−λ​H′​(ρ)−μ⁡(s))=0,∀a,\displaystyle(\text{diag}(Q)-\lambda\text{diag}(H^{\prime})-\mu I)^{\top}\pi=\mathbf{0}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\pi(a|s)(Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)-\lambda H^{\prime}(\rho)-\mu(s))=0,\,\,\forall\,\,a,

This gives the same expression as (19), therefore, the following proof steps are the same as the continuous case. ∎

A.2 Proof of Theorem 4.2

We start by proving the following Lemma:

Lemma A.1.

Define Lπ0π∗(s):=𝔼a∼π∗(⋅|s)[Qπ0(s,a)]L_{\pi_{0}}^{\pi^{*}}(s):=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi^{*}(\cdot|s)}[Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)], consider π∗​(a|s)=[1+ϵ​tanh⁡(A~π02​λ)]​π0​(a|s)\pi^{*}(a|s)=\left[1+\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}}{2\lambda}\right)\right]\pi_{0}(a|s) from Theorem 4.1, we have

Lπ0π∗(s)=Vπ0(s)+ϵ𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[tanh(A~π0​(s,a)2​λ)A~π0(s,a)].\displaystyle L_{\pi_{0}}^{\pi^{*}}(s)=V_{\pi_{0}}(s)+\epsilon\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)}{2\lambda}\right)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)\right].
Proof.

We directly compute Lπ0π∗​(s)L_{\pi_{0}}^{\pi^{*}}(s) as

Lπ0π∗​(s)=𝔼π0​[(1+ϵ​tanh⁡(A~π0​(s,a)2​λ))​Qπ0​(s,a)]\displaystyle L_{\pi_{0}}^{\pi^{*}}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\left(1+\epsilon\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)}{2\lambda}\right)\right)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)\right]
=𝔼π0​[Qπ0​(s,a)]⏟Vπ0​(s)+ϵ​𝔼π0​[tanh⁡(A~π0​(s,a)2​λ)​Qπ0​(s,a)]\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}[Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)]}_{V_{\pi_{0}}(s)}+\epsilon\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)}{2\lambda}\right)Q_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)\right]
=Vπ0​(s)+ϵ​𝔼π0​[tanh⁡(A~π0​(s,a)2​λ)⋅(μ⁡(s)+A~π0​(s,a))]\displaystyle=V_{\pi_{0}}(s)+\epsilon\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)}{2\lambda}\right)\cdot(\mu(s)+\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a))\right]
=Vπ0​(s)+ϵ​𝔼π0​[tanh⁡(A~π0​(s,a)2​λ)​A~π0​(s,a)]+ϵ​𝔼π0​[tanh⁡(A~π0​(s,a)2​λ)]⏟=0​μ​(s).\displaystyle=V_{\pi_{0}}(s)+\epsilon\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)}{2\lambda}\right)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)\right]+\epsilon\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)}{2\lambda}\right)\right]}_{=0}\mu(s).

where we abbreviate 𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)} with 𝔼π0\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}. We have 𝔼π0​[tanh⁡(A~π0​(s,a)2​λ)]=0\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)}{2\lambda}\right)\right]=0 because of the normalization constraint for μ\mu in Theorem 4.1. ∎

We now prove Theorem 4.2 using matrix representations for MDP with a discrete state and action space. The results for continuous spaces can be extended by using linear operators other than matrices.

Proof.

(Theorem 4.2) We define rπ∈ℝ|𝒮|r_{\pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|} with rπ(s):=𝔼a∼π(⋅|s),s′∼P(s′|s,a)[r(s,a,s′)]r_{\pi}(s):=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s),s^{\prime}\sim P(s^{\prime}|s,a)}[r(s,a,s^{\prime})]. The transition kernel Pπ∈ℝ|𝒮|×|𝒮|P_{\pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|\times|\mathcal{S}|} is defined with Pπ(s,s′):=∑a∼π(⋅|s)π(a|s)p(s′|s,a)P_{\pi}(s,s^{\prime}):=\sum_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}\pi(a|s)p(s^{\prime}|s,a). We denote (I−γ​Pπ)−1:=(I+γ​Pπ+γ2​Pπ2+…)(I-\gamma P_{\pi})^{-1}:=(I+\gamma P_{\pi}+\gamma^{2}P_{\pi}^{2}+...). Then, given the initial distribution denoted as d∈[0,1]|𝒮|,d⁡(s):=d0​(s)d\in[0,1]^{|\mathcal{S}|},d(s):=d_{0}(s), we can express the state visitation distribution dπ∈[0,11−γ]|𝒮|d_{\pi}\in[0,\frac{1}{1-\gamma}]^{|\mathcal{S}|} as dπ⊤=d⊤​(I−γ​Pπ)−1d_{\pi}^{\top}=d^{\top}(I-\gamma P_{\pi})^{-1}.

Let us define Vπ∈ℝ|𝒮|V_{\pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}, where each component ss corresponds to Vπ​(s)V_{\pi}(s). The definition of the value function implies that

Vπ=rπ+γ​Pπ​VπVπ=(I−γ​Pπ)−1​rπ.\begin{split}&V_{\pi}=r_{\pi}+\gamma P_{\pi}V_{\pi}\\ &V_{\pi}=(I-\gamma P_{\pi})^{-1}r_{\pi}.\end{split} (20)

We also have

η(π)=𝔼s∼dπ,a∼π(⋅|s),s′∼P(⋅|s,a)[r(s,a,s′)]=d⊤(I−γPπ)−1rπ=d⊤Vπ\eta(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi},a\sim\pi(\cdot|s),s^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot|s,a)}[r(s,a,s^{\prime})]=d^{\top}(I-\gamma P_{\pi})^{-1}r_{\pi}=d^{\top}V_{\pi} (21)

We then define Lπ1π2∈ℝ|𝒮|L^{\pi_{2}}_{\pi_{1}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|} with

Lπ1π2=rπ2+γ​Pπ2​Vπ1,L^{\pi_{2}}_{\pi_{1}}=r_{\pi_{2}}+\gamma P_{\pi_{2}}V_{\pi_{1}}, (22)

which aligns with the definition of Lπ0π∗​(s)L_{\pi_{0}}^{\pi^{*}}(s) in Lemma A.1. Let us denote B1∈ℝ|𝒮|B_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|} with B1(s):=𝔼a∼π0(⋅|s)[tanh(A~π0​(s,a)2​λ)A~π0(s,a)]B_{1}(s):=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)}{2\lambda}\right)\tilde{A}_{\pi_{0}}(s,a)\right]. Then the state-wise result Lemma A.1 can be rewritten for the full state space as

Lπ0π∗=Vπ0+ϵ​B1,L_{\pi_{0}}^{\pi^{*}}=V_{\pi_{0}}+\epsilon B_{1}, (23)

where B1B_{1} is positive along each of its components. Combining (22) and (23) gives

rπ∗+γ​Pπ∗​Vπ0=:Lπ0π∗=Vπ0+ϵ​B1⇒rπ∗=(I−γ​Pπ∗)​Vπ0+ϵ​B1r_{\pi^{*}}+\gamma P_{\pi^{*}}V_{\pi_{0}}=:L_{\pi_{0}}^{\pi^{*}}=V_{\pi_{0}}+\epsilon B_{1}\,\,\Rightarrow\,\,r_{\pi^{*}}=(I-\gamma P_{\pi^{*}})V_{\pi_{0}}+\epsilon B_{1} (24)

On the other hand, applying (20) to π∗\pi^{*} in combination with (24) gives

Corollary A.3 (Asymmetric monotonic performance guarantee).

The optimal policies in Theorem 4.7 satisfy

With Corollary A.3, one can also derive corresponding corollaries for asymmetric BPO like Corollary 4.4 and 4.5.

A.8 Hyperparameters

The hyperparameters for BPO and PPO in RL environments are summarized in Table 2 and Table 3. For the GBPO implementation, we set the discount factor γ=1\gamma=1 and utilize a mini-batch size of 1. Other hyperparameters are the same as those in the original training scripts provided by TTRL [35]. All the experiments are conducted on 4 x NVIDIA H100 GPUs. We set the group size to 32 and the maximum sequence length to 4,096 tokens.

Empirical Tuning Observations: While BPO can generally be initialized using hyperparameters tuned for PPO, specific adjustments often yield superior performance. Empirically, we found that increasing the clip ratio by 0.10.1 and doubling the number of epochs (e.g., from 55 to 1010) can sometimes enhance stability and results. Furthermore, BPO exhibits a higher sensitivity to the entropy coefficient; in many environments, an entropy weight 10−110^{-1} smaller than the optimal PPO setting is sufficient to maintain adequate exploration without destabilizing the policy.
